title: AI Coding Assistants are Getting Smarter - Quantum Computing Report
gist: GQI argues AI-assisted 'vibe coding' will become the primary way people program quantum computers by 2030, pointing to an AI-driven race that cut the resource cost of breaking Bitcoin's ECDSA cryptography by roughly half in four months and to new autonomous AI agents accelerating neutral-atom quantum research.

insights.claim: GQI believes AI-assisted 'vibe coding' will become the primary way people program quantum computers by 2030, based on consensus among the industry experts it speaks with.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Investors in quantum software and developer tools should weight AI-native coding layers over traditional quantum SDKs as the likely long-term programming interface, reshaping where value accrues in the quantum stack.
insights.quote: AI-assisted quantum coding will be the primary way people program quantum computers by 2030.
insights.locator: Most industry experts we speak with agree

insights.claim: Workforce development is quantum computing's central bottleneck: even if a 1-million-qubit quantum computer went online today, few people would know how to program it or exploit its capabilities.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Frames AI coding assistants as solving the 'who will use this' adoption gap, a precondition for commercial quantum ROI that investors should weigh against hardware-only timelines.
insights.locator: Workforce development remains a major concern

insights.claim: The author frames quantum commercial advantage as depending on concurrent progress in both hardware and software, with AI expected to play an increasingly vital role in both.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Reinforces a dual-track investment thesis: value in quantum will accrue not just to qubit-count and fidelity leaders but also to whichever players best harness AI for software and programming tooling.

insights.claim: In April, Google published a whitepaper showing a quantum algorithm that could break the secp256k1 cryptography underlying Bitcoin using only 1,200–1,450 logical qubits and 70–90 million Toffoli gates, an order of magnitude smaller resource requirement than previously thought possible.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Lowers the estimated quantum-hardware bar needed to threaten Bitcoin's cryptography, pulling forward the 'harvest now, decrypt later' risk timeline relevant to crypto-asset custody and post-quantum-migration investment theses.

insights.claim: Google's announcement sparked an AI-driven, hackathon-style race among research groups to further optimize the ECDSA-breaking algorithm, tracked publicly via a 'spacetime score' (Toffoli gates multiplied by qubits, where lower is better) on the site ECDSA.fail.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Gives investors a concrete, trackable public leaderboard metric to monitor as a leading indicator of quantum threat proximity to Bitcoin's cryptography.
insights.locator: Researchers track progress using a spacetime score

insights.claim: Over the past four months, the public ECDSA.fail leaderboard score fell roughly 50%, from Google's initial ~2.9x10^9 to 1.477x10^9, with almost every top-ranking entry achieved using advanced AI models like Claude Opus 4.8 or GPT-5 Codex rather than manual human optimization.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Demonstrates AI models now outperforming human researchers at optimizing quantum attack circuits, evidence that AI is compressing the timeline to a cryptographically relevant quantum threat faster than hardware progress alone would suggest.
insights.quote: almost every top-ranking entry on the leaderboard was achieved using advanced models like Claude Opus 4.8 or GPT-5 Codex
insights.locator: Google's initial algorithm registered a spacetime score

insights.claim: A separate team, doubleAI, used its own AI tool called WarpSpeed to build a circuit breaking ECDSA with 993,181 Toffoli gates and 1,205 qubits, a spacetime score of 1.20x10^9 that is roughly 19% better than the current public leaderboard best, but the result is excluded from the leaderboard because the team published a zero-knowledge proof instead of open-sourcing the code for security reasons.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Signals the true state-of-the-art in breaking Bitcoin's cryptography may already exceed what public leaderboards show, since some teams withhold code for security reasons, so investors should assume the real threat timeline is more advanced than trackers indicate.

insights.claim: A recent arXiv paper from Pasqal and Quantonation describes two AI agents built on Claude models: one automates translating research papers and patents into code optimized for Pasqal's neutral-atom quantum processors, and a second scanned 633 arXiv papers on Rydberg arrays to determine which were executable on current hardware and what upgrades the rest would require.
insights.speaker: Doug Finke
insights.so_what: Illustrates a concrete emerging use case of AI agents autonomously triaging physics literature for hardware-executable experiments, which could dramatically compress the research-to-hardware pipeline for neutral-atom quantum computing specifically.
insights.locator: A recent arXiv paper from Pasqal and Quantonation
